The group-chat dig

One record, everywhere

The sheet you already have becomes the database. The app, the dashboard and the client page all read from it, so nobody types anything twice. Locked saves, rate limits and idempotent writes keep the same booking or task from landing twice.

The human hard drive

Work that chases itself

The copy-paste olympics

Axiom Task Manager

From a weekly meeting log to an app the site team uses.

Client
PT Axiom Construction Co, Bali
Role
Director; designed and delivered it
Team
English and Russian speakers
Timeline
October 2026, ongoing

The gap

Action items buried in a meeting log

Axiom is a team of experienced engineers doing interiors and renovations across four live projects: Villas Seseh, 8SENCE, Angel Cakes Uluwatu and Anantara Dragon. There was no task system. Actions lived inside the weekly protocol, one tab per project, in long status-log cells with no deadlines anyone could track.

The team works in English and Russian, and the protocol had to stay as it was because people still used it every week.

What I built

One record, linked to every stage

A task manager in Google Sheets with Apps Script, then a custom mobile web app on top. The protocol stays the meeting and finance record. The new system holds every action item, linked to its project stage.

How it came together

  1. Task manager in Sheets

    Owners, priorities and status flags with EN⇄RU translation, then an inbox that turns pasted chats into draft tasks.

  2. Protocol migration

    Read the protocol without editing it, extracted every open action and its dated history, linked each to its stage and side.

  3. Protocol view

    A view that reads like the meeting log the team knows, built from the new task data.

  4. Mobile web app

    Built from the team’s feedback: auto-numbering, file uploads, participants, deadlines. Chosen over AppSheet to match the design and cost nothing per user.

KRIYĀ Studio App

The whole studio runs on the sheet it already had.

Client
KRIYĀ tattoo studio, Bali
Role
Owner; designed and built it
Built on
The studio’s existing Main Sheet
Timeline
August to November 2026

The gap

A working sheet that made people retype everything

The studio already ran on a Google Sheet: a bookings log, a client CRM and an income dashboard. But a single booking meant twelve typed fields, clients entered twice, and prices and commission worked out by hand. Quotes lived in DMs, nobody could see who had done what that day, and nothing caught two clients booked into the same chair.

What I built

One link, three pages, the same sheet underneath

The team app, behind a studio code, gives everyone a daily checklist, a team view of who is done, tasks that can’t be marked blocked without saying what they wait on, a quote calculator for walk-ins and DMs, bookings with clash warnings, and open books where each person sees their own commission.

The request page is public. Clients describe their idea and see a rough price range before they even ask.

A private quote page goes to each client with a secret key in its link. They accept and pick a day, or make an offer. Offers below the low end of the quote go to the owner. The team gets an email either way.

The gap

Lessons and practice lived in different places

A student learning Indonesian from Russian had good lessons and generic apps, and nothing connecting the two. Words taught on Tuesday never showed up in Wednesday’s practice, and the teacher couldn’t see what had stuck.

What I built

One app, two sides of the same lesson

Students sign up, wait for approval, then practise word decks with spaced repetition and read short stories with questions. They switch between English and Russian explanations.

The teacher approves students, logs the words taught in each lesson, keeps private notes, and writes decks and stories in the app instead of code. A word logged after class appears in that student’s Dari guru (“from the teacher”) deck straight away.

Students get reasons to come back: a Today screen with a daily goal and a word of the day, two games (Match Rush, six pairs against the clock, and Cat Hunt, a pixel game starring three real cats), stories where any word can be tapped to translate and save, and a Memory view that turns Ebbinghaus’s forgetting curve into a personal recall estimate.

It started as a lean practice app for one learner and grew into a platform for several students in the same week, without changing hosts or adding a server.

Untracked spend by period

Rupiah and receipts
Tap a period for detail
TotalRp1.043.00039

What I built

Three systems the team already used, made into one record

Receipts arrived in a WhatsApp group. The ledger was a Google Sheet with a tab per month and a tab per person. Files belonged in month-dated Drive folders. Nothing connected them, so receipts sat in the chat until someone found time to scroll back.

The automation drove the WhatsApp desktop app directly, exported each receipt, and prepared a dated ledger row for it, with the file linked into the Receipt column as a chip.

  1. WhatsApp group
  2. Export receipt
  3. Drive, RECEIPTS / OCT 2026
  4. Ledger row and chip

The house rules

It followed the house rules already in the sheet

Categories, payment types, the DD/MM/YYYY date format and the tab layout were all read from rows the team had already written. The hardest rule was never written down: receipts print street addresses, while the team says nicknames. Matching the same address across different messages rebuilt that map, so later receipts filed themselves by address alone.

Five discrepancies a first pass missed

Receipt skipped entirely1
“Missing”, actually scrolled past2
Route misread from a caption2

Caught by re-checking every cluster boundary against WhatsApp’s document index, and the original PDF where a caption disagreed.

Human checkpoints

Two calls went back to a person instead of being guessed: a backlog of rides booked under an unfamiliar staff name, and two rides the ride app itself marked Profile: PERSONAL. Both were flagged and kept out of the ledger.

The time saved is measured against a teammate’s average DeskTime activity in Google Sheets for tracking these expenses, uploading receipts and updating the petty cash sheet by hand.

    House rules

    Ten rules every build follows. Short enough to remember, strict enough to matter.

    1. Build on what already works.
    2. Every number on the page must be checkable.
    3. If the team won’t open it, it doesn’t exist.
    4. Speak the team’s languages, all of them.
    5. Ask the person doing the work, not only the person paying for it.
    6. No new subscription without a very good reason.
    7. Fix the boring part first. It’s usually the expensive part.
    8. Write it down before you forget why.
    9. Leave the owner able to run it without me.
    10. Never automate a mess. Tidy it, then automate it.

    The oldest system on the island

    For about a thousand years, Bali’s rice farmers have shared water through the subak: a network of canals, cooperatives and water temples that decides who floods their fields, and when.

    In the 1970s the Green Revolution brought a new plan: plant as often as you can and ignore the temple calendar. Within a year or two the pests moved in and the water ran short.

    Years later, an anthropologist named Stephen Lansing ran the numbers. When neighbouring fields flood and go fallow together, the pests starve. The temple schedule had been doing the pest control all along, and it worked better than its replacement. The old way came back, and in 2012 UNESCO made it a World Heritage landscape.

    I build with that in mind. The system your people already run usually knows something you can’t see from outside, and my job is to give it better tools.

    What people ask first

    How much does it cost?

    It depends on the gap. If a build would cost more than the hours it gives back, I’ll tell you not to do it. You get a price after the first conversation.

    Do we have to switch software?

    No. Whatever your team runs on today, a spreadsheet, a group chat, an old CRM or a paper logbook, that’s what I build on. Nothing gets ripped out.

    How fast is fast?

    Ludwig went from a first question to a working teaching platform in a day. Bigger systems, like Axiom’s migration from a weekly meeting log, take a few weeks of real use and feedback.

    My team speaks three languages. Problem?

    Not for the app. It works in any language your team speaks, and translations never overwrite what a person wrote.

    Who owns it when you’re done?

    You. It lives in your Google account or your own Supabase project, not mine, with a guide your team can follow.

    When isn’t this a fit?

    When you want a forty-page strategy deck and nothing that runs on Monday.
